title: RAG, retrieval permissions, and serving tradeoffs
summary: Give an assistant relevant documents before it answers. Trace which documents enter the prompt, keep permissions attached, and understand what retrieval and caching cannot guarantee.
objectives: Separate document ingestion from online retrieval and generation.
Place authorization before private text reaches the model.
Explain stale documents, grounded-answer evaluation, and safe cache boundaries.

terms.definition: Retrieval-augmented generation: retrieve relevant material and provide it to a model as context for an answer.
A selected portion of a document stored and retrieved as a unit.
A numeric representation used to compare similarity; it does not encode permission or truth.
Connecting an answer to supporting source material.
Reordering an initial candidate set with a more focused relevance method.
Reusing previously computed serving state for a matching input prefix; this is different from caching a final answer.

retrieval: Where did the search system enforce access before exposing snippets?
Why can a fluent model output still be wrong?

sections.title: Give the assistant a relevant reading packet
sections.markdown:
A company assistant answers questions about internal procedures. The model's training is not a live database of the company's current documents. Instead, retrieve a small relevant reading packet and include it with the question. The model can then produce an answer using that packet and point to its sources.

Think of asking a researcher to answer with selected pages from a library. Better pages make the task easier, but the researcher can still misunderstand them. Choosing pages also does not decide who may read them. Relevance, permission, and correctness are separate questions.

Our first product answers questions; it does not execute instructions from the documents. A document may contain quoted commands, outdated guidance, or malicious instructions. Treat retrieved text as evidence to examine, not as a higher-priority instruction that can change the application's rules.

sections.title: Prepare documents with their identities intact
sections.markdown:
Ingestion prepares searchable pieces without losing what they mean or who may read them.

| Chunk field | Example | Why keep it? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Source identity | room-policy | Find the authoritative document |
| Document version | 6 | Distinguish current evidence from old text |
| Location | “Opening hours,” paragraph 2 | Show supporting context and citation |
| Access reference | staff-policy scope | Apply the required audience check |
| Text | Rule plus its relevant exception | Avoid a misleading fragment |

Choose meaningful boundaries. Separating “open until 18:00” from “except Friday, until 16:00” can retrieve the rule while losing the condition needed by the question.

Embeddings help locate semantically related text; keyword search helps exact names, numbers, and unusual identifiers. A hybrid design can use both. Similarity does not prove truth or permission.

Updates and deletions must reach the derived index. Store versions and indexing progress, define a freshness target, and prevent old chunks from indefinitely claiming to be current. Rebuilds need the same supported snapshot/catch-up reasoning as other derived views.

sections.title: Follow one private question through the system
sections.markdown:
A logged-in employee asks, “What is the travel limit for my team?” First, identify the tenant and user's current access scope. Second, retrieve candidates using appropriate scope filtering. Third, validate the access policy for any private text that will be exposed or sent to the model.

Fourth, select or rerank useful passages, bound their total size, and construct the prompt. Fifth, generate an answer with source references and a way to say that evidence is missing.

Authorization must happen before restricted text reaches the model, not merely before the browser displays the final answer. Asking the model to ignore a forbidden passage after including it is not a privacy control. Logging and traces also need the same care: a debug record containing the hidden passage is still a disclosure path.

Permission revocation is a difficult freshness case. A stale copied access list may keep allowing a removed user. Revalidate against current authority or implement a propagation design whose revocation guarantee the product explicitly accepts. Cached retrieval results and generated answers must not bypass that check.

sections.title: Find which stage lost the answer
sections.markdown:
Suppose the correct policy document exists but the assistant gives the wrong travel limit. Inspect the stages separately. Did ingestion capture the latest version? Did retrieval include the relevant paragraph and exception? Did authorization correctly allow the employee? Did the model use the supplied evidence rather than invent a number?

Keep a judged question set with expected evidence and access scope. Test retrieval coverage, answer support, citation correctness, and appropriate abstention when documents disagree or lack the answer. A citation is a navigational aid, not automatic proof that the cited passage supports the sentence.

For a concrete failure test, give tenant A a document titled “Travel policy” with limit 500 and tenant B a different document of the same title with limit 900. Ask the same question in both scopes, then revoke one user's access. A global cache keyed only by question text can fail both tenant isolation and revocation even if retrieval itself was correct.

sections.title: Cache the right thing under the right assumptions
sections.markdown:
Two caches reuse different things.

| Cache | Reuses | Must still be decided |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Final-answer cache | Previously generated text | Audience, document versions, model/template versions, freshness and revocation |
| Serving prefix cache | Matching-prefix computation state | Serving compatibility, isolation, memory policy, and new output work |

Question text alone is not a safe key for a private answer. The same sentence can have different permitted evidence for different people.

A prefix cache does not establish correctness or make generation free. It may reduce repeated input processing while later decoding still occurs. Sharing state also needs appropriate isolation and side-channel consideration under the actual implementation.

**Interview phrase:** “I will state what is being reused and under which audience and version conditions.” Then trace a document update, a permission revocation, and a question with no supporting evidence.

Vector-index internals and fine-grained GPU scheduling are optional depth after the derived-data and trust story is sound.

diagrams.source:

exercise.prompt: Two companies ask the identical question but have different private policies. Draw where the tenant and user permissions apply. A user then loses access while an answer remains cached. Explain the safe cache behavior and one quality test.
rubric: Enforce permission before model input and before returning cached private content.
Bind cache validity to relevant scope/versions and revocation policy.
Test whether cited evidence actually supports the answer for the correct tenant.
exercise.solution: Carry tenant and user identity through retrieval and enforce current policy before private chunks enter the prompt. A cached answer must remain valid for this audience and document/permission state; invalidate or reauthorize it when access changes. Never use question text alone as a private-answer cache key. Test two same-title policy documents with different values, check the correct tenant’s evidence, and verify that the revoked user receives no private answer. Separately check that each citation supports its associated claim.

questions.prompt: A prefix cache is the same as a final-answer cache.
questions.explanation: It reuses serving computation for an input prefix rather than necessarily reusing the generated answer.

questions.prompt: Why test retrieval and generation separately?
questions.answer: Missing or stale evidence is a different failure from a model ignoring correct evidence. Stage-specific tests reveal which mechanism needs improvement.
questions.explanation: Missing or stale evidence is a different failure from a model ignoring correct evidence. Stage-specific tests reveal which mechanism needs improvement.

walkthroughs.title: Follow evidence that changes the answer
walkthroughs.intro: An authorized staff member asks when a study room closes on Friday. The permitted policy has a general rule and a nearby exception.

steps.title: Establish the question and audience
steps.explanation: The service resolves the current access scope before deciding which private passages may enter a prompt.

steps.title: Retrieve complete supporting context
steps.explanation: The selected permitted evidence from version 6 includes both the ordinary hours and Friday exception.

steps.title: Construct bounded model context
steps.explanation: The model receives the allowed passage with its source location. Retrieved text remains evidence, not authority to perform actions.

steps.title: Check the supported answer
steps.explanation: The response should use the Friday condition and point to the supporting passage. A citation is inspected for support rather than accepted as proof by itself.

walkthroughs.takeaway: Retrieval quality includes preserving the condition that changes the answer. Permission and source support remain separate checks.
